chapter_title: The Raven and the Fox (Fables and Folk Tales)
subject: English
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 4 periods = 160 minutes
Total: 4 periods · 2h 40min

periods.activity_title: Reading the Beast Fable: Flattery and Foolish Pride

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss I (p.14): fill in blanks stanza by stanza, all four stanzas.
Let us discuss II (p.15): match seven words from poem to their meanings.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the poem aloud (p.13–14), students follow in their textbooks. Pause briefly after each stanza to let the rhythm and rhyming couplets land — limb/him, beak/seek, word/bird — before moving on.

Work through “Let us discuss I” (p.14) stanza by stanza as a whole-class activity. Students call out answers; teacher confirms and briefly explains each choice, drawing attention to the Raven’s pride and the Fox’s cunning as the engine of the poem.

Students complete “Let us discuss II” (p.15) individually — matching the seven vocabulary words to their meanings — then pairs compare. Take brief whole-class feedback, highlighting how words like ‘morsel’ and ‘eyed’ build the Fox’s desire.

periods.teacher_notes: The poem’s humour depends on students grasping that the Raven genuinely believes the Fox’s praise — stress the phrase ‘foolish pride’ during the read-aloud so this motivation is clear. A common misreading is that the Raven is simply careless; redirect students to Stanza 3 where the text says he ‘forgot that his voice was just a croak’, showing it is pride, not inattention, that costs him his food. Tasks on identifying the tone of the Fox’s flattery in ‘Let us think and reflect II’ (p.16) are not covered in class today and may be explored as self-study.

periods.activity_title: Listening to the Crow’s Resolve, Then Retelling the Fable

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us listen (p.18): mark three statements true or false as teacher reads transcript.
Let us speak (p.18): narrate poem as a story with a different ending.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the listening transcript (p.37) aloud at a steady pace while students listen with books closed. Students then open to p.18 and mark the three statements true or false; teacher reads the transcript once more for checking, then the class verifies each verdict together.

Teacher models the speaking prompt from “Let us speak” (p.18) using the given opening line — ‘This is a story about a clever fox named Reynard and Mr Raven. One day…’ — narrating the first two stanzas as a story. Students are given a quiet moment to plan their alternative ending mentally.

Three or four volunteers narrate the fable aloud with their own endings while the class listens. Encourage brief appreciative responses from the audience — what made an ending surprising or satisfying? — to keep the activity dialogic.

periods.teacher_notes: The listening transcript (p.37) uses the word ‘crow’ for the bird protagonist; let students know this is the same character as the Raven before you begin, so they are not confused. When students narrate their alternative endings, the most common shortfall is abandoning the moral entirely — prompt any student who does so by asking what lesson their Raven or Fox would carry away from the new ending.

periods.activity_title: Dialogue Writing and the Language of the Poem

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us write (p.18): write the fable’s events as a dialogue script, Raven acting only.
Let us learn (p.16): identify rhyming word pairs from all four stanzas.

homework.task_brief: Let us learn (p.17): match each word to its opposite from the given box.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the “Let us write” prompt (p.18) aloud and shows the model opening on the board: Reynard’s line followed by ‘(Mr Raven just nods his head)’. Discuss briefly why the Raven can only use stage directions — he holds food in his beak — so students understand the constraint before they draft.

Students write their dialogue scripts individually, covering the whole arc of the poem: Fox’s flattery, Raven’s reactions in stage directions, the food falling, and Fox’s parting words. Teacher circulates, prompting students to match their dialogue to each stanza’s event and to use the Fox’s voice from the poem.

Two pairs quickly read out their scripts as a cold read — one student as Fox, another narrating the Raven’s actions. Brief class feedback: does the Fox sound flattering enough? Does the ending carry the moral?

Open the textbook to “Let us learn” (p.16). Students locate and write the rhyming word pairs from each of the four stanzas. Teacher confirms on the board, noting how couplet rhyme (limb/him, beak/seek) drives the poem’s brisk, fable-like rhythm.

periods.teacher_notes: The writing task asks students to suppress the Raven’s speech entirely — a deliberate constraint that mirrors the poem’s drama. Watch for students who give the Raven spoken lines; redirect them to the stage-direction format shown in the model opening. The rhyming-pairs task in ‘Let us learn’ (p.16) connects naturally to what students just wrote: the couplet pairs they identify are the backbone of the poem’s tone and pace. The alliteration task (p.17) and the opposites table (p.17) are not covered in class; the opposites matching is set for homework.
materials: Blank paper or exercise books for dialogue drafts

periods.activity_title: Alliteration, Word Study, and Puppet Performance

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.17): identify alliteration in Stanza 2 of the poem.
Let us explore (p.19): make origami stick puppets and enact the poem.

time_bands.activity: Review the concept of alliteration using the two examples given in “Let us learn” (p.17) — ‘great big beak’ and ‘song of sweet birds’. Students then scan Stanza 2 of the poem and identify one further example of alliteration, sharing their answers aloud and explaining the repeated sound.

Students use the step-by-step pictures on p.19 to fold and assemble origami stick puppets of the Raven and the Fox. Teacher moves around the room helping with folding steps; students may also help each other. Each student should have both puppets ready before the performance phase.

Pairs or small groups enact the poem using their puppets — one student voices the Fox’s flattery, another holds the Raven puppet and performs the actions. Encourage the Fox’s final moralising speech to be delivered with comic flourish, reinforcing the poem’s central lesson about pride and flattery.

periods.teacher_notes: When students search Stanza 2 for alliteration, the intended example is the ‘such feathers’ / ‘sweet birds’ cluster — accept any well-reasoned answer that names the repeated consonant sound clearly. The puppet enactment brings the poem’s beast-fable tradition to life and gives physical expression to the tone shift from admiring flattery to ironic triumph; let the performance be playful and allow brief improvisation in the Fox’s final speech.

items.item_stem: In the poem “The Raven and the Fox”, Reynard praises the Raven’s feathers and suggests that the birds of the woods would call the Raven their King if he were to sing. Which of the following best explains why Reynard makes this suggestion?

options.label: A
options.text: Reynard genuinely believes the Raven has a beautiful singing voice.

options.label: B
options.text: Reynard hopes the other forest birds will come and share the food.

options.label: C
options.text: Reynard is trying to teach the Raven a lesson about pride from the start.

options.label: D
options.text: Reynard wants the Raven to open his beak so the morsel will fall.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Students who choose this miss the Fox’s cunning — he only pretends to admire the Raven’s voice.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Suggests a misreading of the scene; the Fox wants the morsel for himself, not to attract others.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Confuses the Fox’s deliberate deception with a planned moral lesson, which comes only after he has the food.

items.item_stem: In the final stanza of “The Raven and the Fox”, the Fox laughs and tells the Raven that pride is “rather unwise”. Do you think the Fox is being sincere in this teaching, or is he using the moral as one more act of mockery? Use evidence from the poem to support your view.

expected_elements: States a clear view — sincere or mocking — with a reason.
Cites the Fox’s laughter (‘Ha-ha!’) or his earlier flattery as evidence.
Connects the Fox’s character (cunning, self-serving) to the interpretation offered.

items.item_stem: Listen to the passage about what the crow did after losing his food. Then decide whether each of the following statements is true or false.

options.text: After losing his food, the crow felt sad and thought about what had happened.
The crow decided to stay at home and keep his wisdom to himself.
The crow told other animals not to let pride cause them to lose what they have.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer:
1. True — the transcript says the crow felt really sad and thought to himself about being fooled by kind words.
2. False — the crow decided to go on a journey to share his wisdom with other animals.
3. True — the transcript states the crow told them, ‘Do not let pride lose what you have.’

items.item_stem: In the passage you listened to, the crow says he has learned something important even though he was tricked. In one or two sentences, explain what the crow learned about himself and what he decided to do with that learning.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The crow learned that even without beautiful feathers he is smart, and that being tricked by kind words was a valuable lesson. He decided to journey to other animals and share the warning that pride can cost you what you value.

items.item_stem: Recount the events of “The Raven and the Fox” as a spoken story in your own words. Begin with how Reynard noticed the Raven on the branch, and end with the moment the morsel fell. Speak clearly so your listener can follow the sequence of events.

expected_elements: Covers three key events: Raven on branch with food, Fox’s flattery, Raven opening beak.
Names both characters — Reynard the Fox and Mr Raven — correctly.
Narrates in a logical sequence with connecting words (then, next, finally).
Uses a clear, audible speaking voice appropriate for storytelling.

items.item_stem: Imagine that in a different version of this fable, the Raven does not drop his food. Give a short spoken response: what would the Raven say to Reynard, and what lesson would this new ending teach? Give a reason for your choice of lesson.

expected_elements: Invents a plausible spoken reply for the Raven that shows he sees through the flattery.
States a clear alternative moral or lesson arising from the new ending.
Gives a reason explaining why this lesson follows from the events described.
Speaks with appropriate expression, distinguishing the Raven’s voice from narration.

items.item_stem: Write the opening exchange of the fable as a dialogue script. Include Reynard’s first two flattering speeches and the Raven’s reactions as stage directions in brackets. Use the format: Character name: spoken words / (action in brackets). Your script should cover the events of the first two stanzas only.

expected_elements: Uses correct script format — speaker name followed by colon and speech.
Raven’s responses are only stage directions in brackets, no spoken words.
Reynard’s lines reflect flattery about feathers and the suggestion of singing.
Covers events from both stanzas one and two in the correct order.

items.item_stem: Write the final scene of the fable as a dialogue script, beginning from the moment the morsel falls to the ground. Reynard should deliver his moralising speech in his own voice. You may choose to give the Raven a spoken line at the very end — or keep him silent — but explain your choice in a sentence after the script.

expected_elements: Script shows the morsel falling and Reynard’s triumphant speech capturing the moral about pride.
Reynard’s dialogue reflects the tone of ironic triumph from the poem’s final stanza.
Student makes a clear choice about the Raven’s final voice and gives a reason.
Script format is consistent — speaker names, colons, stage directions in brackets where needed.

limb|seek
beak|him
word|sing

items.item_stem: Read the lines on page 13 beginning “Sir Raven, you are a handsome bird.” Stanza 2 of the poem contains an example of alliteration. Identify the alliterative phrase from Stanza 2, name the repeated consonant sound, and explain in one sentence how this sound adds to the effect of the Fox’s flattery.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The alliterative phrase in Stanza 2 is ‘sweet birds’ (or ‘Sir… sing’ — accept any phrase from Stanza 2 with a clearly identified repeated consonant). The soft, flowing sound of the repeated consonant mirrors the smoothness and pleasantness of the Fox’s flattering words.

items.item_stem: Using paper and a stick or pencil, make a simple stick puppet of either the Raven or the Fox from the poem. Then, using your puppet, perform the speech your character gives in the poem — Reynard’s flattering words to the Raven, or the Fox’s moralising laughter at the end. Speak the lines from memory or in your own words.

expected_elements: Puppet is recognisable as the chosen character — Raven or Fox.
Student performs the character’s speech with appropriate tone — flattering or triumphant.
Spoken lines are faithful to the poem’s events and the character’s role.
Performance shows engagement with the poem’s central theme of pride and flattery.

items.item_stem: Beast fables like “The Raven and the Fox” use animal characters to teach human lessons. Think of another animal pair — one clever and one easily flattered — and describe in a short paragraph: what the clever animal wants, what flattery it uses, and what moral your new fable would teach. You do not need to write the full fable, only the plan.

expected_elements: Names a clear animal pair with distinct roles — one crafty, one vain.
Describes a believable flattery the crafty animal uses to manipulate the other.
States a moral that logically follows from the imagined events.
Shows understanding of beast fable conventions drawn from the poem.
